references.text: The verse provides the context for the prohibition against touching the mountain and the warning of death for anyone who crosses the boundary.
After the covenant was established, selected individuals were permitted to go up on the mountain, in contrast to the prohibition in Exodus 19:13.
Stoning is mentioned as the penalty for death, the same method described in Exodus 19:13.
Stoning outside the camp as punishment for blasphemy, parallel to the stoning penalty mentioned in the verse.
The jubilee horn (shofar) is used to call the people together, as in Exodus 19:13 where the sound of the horn signals that the people may go up.
The jubilee horn was used at the fall of Jericho, the same horn mentioned in Exodus 19:13.
The letter to the Hebrews refers directly to this event and warns that even an animal that touched the mountain was to be stoned.
Both verses describe the boundaries of the sanctuary at Mount Sinai; 19:13 establishes the penalty for violation, while 34:3 emphasizes the necessity of keeping all that is profane away.
The letter to the Hebrews explicitly quotes Exodus 19:13 to illustrate the fear associated with the old covenant and the contrast with grace in the new.
